questions.stem: In 'The Daemon Lover', what happens on the narrator's wedding day?
options: Her fiance's wife arrives at the flat and tells her the truth about him
Her fiance, Jamie Harris, never arrives, and she searches the city for him
Her fiance, Jamie Harris, arrives drunk, and she calls off the wedding
Her mother forbids the marriage, and she runs away to the city on her own
questions.explanation: Jamie Harris is meant to collect her for the wedding but never comes. She spends the day asking shopkeepers and strangers about him, and the reader begins to wonder whether he ever existed.

questions.stem: How does 'The Daemon Lover' end?
options: She keeps returning to a door where she hears voices, but no one ever answers
She finds Jamie at a newsstand and he promises to marry her the next morning
She learns from the police that Jamie has been killed in a car accident
She goes home, burns all his letters and decides she is better off alone
questions.explanation: The search ends at a run-down building where she believes Jamie has gone. She hears voices and laughter behind a door and keeps coming back to knock, but no one ever answers. The ending leaves her trapped in waiting.

questions.stem: In 'Like Mother Used to Make', David Turner cooks dinner for his neighbour Marcia. What happens when Mr Harris arrives?
options: Mr Harris offers David a job at the office where Marcia works
Marcia acts as if David's apartment and cooking are hers
Mr Harris reveals that he is Marcia's husband from out of town
David asks Mr Harris to leave, and Marcia goes with him
questions.explanation: Marcia plays hostess in David's neat apartment and even claims his cherry pie. David is too polite to object, so he slowly loses his own home.

questions.stem: How does 'Like Mother Used to Make' end?
options: David throws Marcia and Mr Harris out and locks his apartment door
David moves out of the building and finds a new place across town
David tells Mr Harris the truth, and Marcia apologises to him
David lets himself into Marcia's messy apartment and starts to clean it
questions.explanation: Marcia hands David the key to her own flat and thanks him for dinner as if he were the guest. He ends up alone in her dirty apartment, tidying it, while they talk in his.

questions.stem: In 'The Villager', Hilda Clarence visits the Roberts apartment to look at furniture for sale. What does she do when Mr Harris arrives?
options: She recognises him as a man who once rejected her as a dancer
She hides in the bedroom until he gives up and leaves the flat
She lets him think she is Nancy Roberts and claims to be a dancer
She tells him the furniture is already sold and asks him to leave
questions.explanation: Mr Harris assumes Hilda is Mrs Roberts, and she plays along. For a few minutes she lives the life she once wanted, which shows how far her real life has fallen short of her dreams.

questions.stem: What had Hilda Clarence come to New York hoping to be, and what did she become?
options: A painter; she became a schoolteacher instead
A writer; she became a literary agent instead
A dancer; she became a stenographer instead
An actress; she became a waitress instead
questions.explanation: Hilda arrived as a young woman wanting to dance, but took office work to support herself and gave up her ambition.

questions.stem: In 'The Witch', what does the old man on the train tell four-year-old Johnny?
options: A story about a witch who lives in a house beside the railway line
A warning that the train will crash before it reaches the city
A secret that Johnny's mother is not really his mother at all
A story about hurting his own little sister, which Johnny enjoys
questions.explanation: The stranger starts kindly, then calmly describes violence against his sister. Johnny laughs and is delighted, while his mother is horrified. The story suggests that cruelty can delight even a small child.

questions.stem: In 'The Renegade', Mrs Walpole's dog Lady is accused of killing a neighbour's chickens. How does the town respond?
options: Neighbours offer cruel 'cures' with growing relish, and her children repeat them gleefully
Neighbours ignore the problem until the police arrive to take the dog away
Neighbours ask Mrs Walpole to pay for the chickens, and the matter is closed
Neighbours defend Lady and blame a fox that has been seen near the farm
questions.explanation: Everyone Mrs Walpole meets has advice, each idea crueller than the last, such as a spiked collar. Her own twins describe it with delight. The ordinary community enjoys the idea of violence.

questions.stem: In 'After You, My Dear Alphonse', what does Mrs Wilson assume about her son Johnny's friend Boyd?
options: That his family is poor, so she offers him secondhand clothes
That he is a bad influence, so she sends him home before lunch
That he has stolen the kindling he is carrying from her woodpile
That he is older than Johnny, so she asks him to look after him
questions.explanation: Mrs Wilson assumes that because Boyd is Black his family must be struggling. In fact his father is a foreman and his sister plans to be a teacher. Boyd politely declines the clothes, and her 'kindness' exposes her prejudice.

questions.stem: What is the twist at the end of 'Charles'?
options: There is no Charles in the kindergarten: the stories were about Laurie
Charles is the teacher's son, which is why he is never punished
Charles has been expelled, and Laurie misses him terribly
Charles is Laurie's older cousin, who visits the kindergarten each week
questions.explanation: Laurie comes home every day with tales of a naughty boy called Charles. At the parent meeting the teacher tells his mother there is no Charles, so the bad behaviour was Laurie's own.

questions.stem: In 'Flower Garden', why does the town turn against Mrs MacLane?
options: She hires Mr Jones, a Black man, to work in her garden
She refuses to send her son Davey to the local school
She buys the Winning family's house without asking them
She lets her garden grow wild and spoils the neighbourhood
questions.explanation: Mrs MacLane, a widow new to town, hires Mr Jones and is kind to his son. The town quietly shuns her, and Mrs Winning, who had befriended her, joins in. The story exposes racism behind polite manners.

questions.stem: In 'Elizabeth', what does Elizabeth Style do after Robert Shax hires a young receptionist, Daphne?
options: She fires Daphne and arranges dinner with James Harris, hoping he will change her life
She resigns from the agency and goes home to her family in the country
She asks Daphne to share her apartment so that they can save on rent
She leaves Robert for a new job at a large publishing company
questions.explanation: Elizabeth is a partner in Robert's small literary agency and also his lover. Threatened by Daphne, she fires her and pins her hopes on Jim Harris, a writer she barely knows.

questions.stem: In 'Of Course', what does Mrs Harris tell her new neighbour, Mrs Tylor, about her husband?
options: He does not allow movies or the radio in their home
He works nights, so the children must be quiet all day
He is a minister, so the family cannot play on Sundays
He is travelling, so she will be alone for several months
questions.explanation: Mrs Tylor keeps answering 'of course' as Mrs Harris explains her husband's strict rules. The polite phrase hides judgement and unease, and shows how social courtesy can mask real feeling.

questions.stem: Why does Clara Spencer travel to New York in 'The Tooth'?
options: To meet a man named Jim she had written to
To have an aching tooth treated by a dentist
To visit her husband, who works in the city
To sign the papers for her late father's estate
questions.explanation: Clara takes a night bus to the city with a painful tooth. On the way she meets a stranger, Jim, who talks of a distant place, and after the extraction she loses her sense of who she is.

questions.stem: On what date, in 'The Lottery', does the village hold the lottery?
options: December 31st, at midnight in the square
June 27th, on a clear and sunny morning
June 26th, on a cold and rainy morning
July 4th, during the village's celebrations
questions.explanation: The story opens on a beautiful summer morning, with flowers blooming and grass green. The pleasant setting makes the violent ending more shocking.

questions.stem: Who conducts the lottery?
options: Mr Summers, who runs the coal business
Mr Graves, who owns the general store
Old Man Warner, the village's oldest man
Mr Adams, who leads the village council
questions.explanation: Mr Summers, a jovial man who runs many civic events, conducts the lottery, helped by the postmaster, Mr Graves. His cheerful manner makes the ritual seem routine.

questions.stem: What do we learn about the black box used in the lottery?
options: It is the original box from the first lottery, carefully repaired by every family
It is shabby, but the villagers will not replace it, and paper slips have replaced wood chips
It is new each year, built by Mr Graves to keep the slips of paper fair and secret
It is kept in the church, and only the minister is allowed to open it on the day
questions.explanation: The box is splintered and faded, yet no one wants to upset tradition by making a new one. Much of the ritual has already been forgotten, which shows that the village clings to tradition without understanding it.

questions.stem: How is Tessie Hutchinson chosen?
options: Bill draws the marked slip for the family, then Tessie draws the black spot
Tessie arrives last, so the rules say she must take the final slip of paper
Old Man Warner chooses her because she complained about the lottery
The villagers vote for her after she argues with Mr Summers in public
questions.explanation: The lottery has two stages. First each household's head draws, and Bill Hutchinson gets the marked slip. Then every member of his family draws, and Tessie's slip has the black spot.

questions.stem: What role does Old Man Warner play in 'The Lottery'?
options: He is chosen in the lottery and accepts his fate without a word
He defends the lottery and scorns villages that have given it up
He questions the lottery and is the first to refuse to throw a stone
He runs the lottery and keeps the black box in his barn all year
questions.explanation: Warner has taken part in the lottery for seventy-seven years and calls those who would stop it fools. He stands for blind loyalty to tradition.

questions.stem: Why is Tessie Hutchinson's protest at the end of 'The Lottery' ironic?
options: She objects because she wants the lottery moved to a day that suits her household better
She objects on behalf of the children, although she has no children of her own
She objects only once her family is chosen, and even tries to add her married daughter's family
She objects to the lottery every year, but the village has never listened to her before
questions.explanation: Tessie arrives cheerfully and has accepted the lottery all her life. She cries that it is unfair only when it threatens her, and she tries to make Don and Eva take their chance too.

questions.stem: Mrs Delacroix chats warmly with Tessie early in 'The Lottery', then picks a stone so large she needs both hands. What does this show?
options: That Mrs Delacroix has secretly hated Tessie for many years
That Mrs Delacroix is forced by Mr Summers to throw first
That the villagers choose the strongest person to begin
How quickly friendly neighbours become part of the violence
questions.explanation: The friendly gossip and the heavy stone come from the same woman. Jackson suggests that cruelty does not need villains; ordinary, likeable people take part when the community expects it.

questions.stem: Characters named James Harris, or Harris, appear in several of the set stories. What is the effect?
options: It suggests the stories form a single novel with one continuous plot
It presents Harris as a dependable figure who rescues lonely women
It shows Harris as a comic villain whose schemes are finally exposed
It links the stories through a charming, elusive figure who draws people from their lives
questions.explanation: Jamie Harris in 'The Daemon Lover', Jim Harris in 'Elizabeth' and the stranger Jim in 'The Tooth' all seem to promise escape. The collection ends with the old ballad 'The Daemon Lover', about a demon lover called James Harris.

questions.stem: Where was 'The Lottery' first published, and how did readers respond?
options: In a London newspaper in 1952; readers asked for a happier ending
In a horror magazine in 1939; readers voted it their favourite story
In The New Yorker in 1948; many readers sent angry or confused letters
In a school anthology in 1960; many teachers asked for it to be removed
questions.explanation: The story appeared in June 1948 and drew a flood of letters, many angry or bewildered. Some readers even asked where such lotteries were held, a sign of how real its ordinary setting felt.

questions.stem: Several sections of the collection open with quotations from a 17th-century book by Joseph Glanvill. What is the book about?
options: Shipwrecks
Etiquette
Witchcraft
Gardening
questions.explanation: The epigraphs come from Saducismus Triumphatus, a book defending belief in witches. They frame the ordinary stories with ideas of witchcraft, persecution and the devil in daily life.

questions.stem: 'After You, My Dear Alphonse' and 'Flower Garden' are set in late-1940s America. Which feature of that society do they expose?
options: Anti-communist suspicion of neighbours in the early Cold War
The poverty of farming families during the Great Depression
Class resentment between factory workers and their bosses
Racial prejudice hidden behind polite, respectable behaviour
questions.explanation: Both stories show white middle-class characters who see themselves as kind but act on racist assumptions. Jackson exposes prejudice in manners, gossip and exclusion rather than in open violence.

questions.stem: Many set stories centre on women in the home or women alone in the city in the late 1940s. What pressure do they reveal?
options: Expectations that women should marry, keep house and conform to their community
Laws that stopped women from living alone or working in offices in New York
A shortage of housing that forced women to share apartments with strangers
The demand that women return to factory work after the war had ended
questions.explanation: Tessie, Mrs Winning, Mrs Walpole, Elizabeth and the bride in 'The Daemon Lover' are judged by how well they fit expected roles. Fear of not fitting in drives much of their behaviour.

questions.stem: Which idea is most central to 'The Lottery'?
options: The struggle of wives against the authority of their husbands
The danger of following tradition without questioning it
The way the harvest depends on the community's sacrifices
The cruelty of one leader who forces his will on a village
questions.explanation: The villagers have forgotten the ritual's purpose and much of its form, yet keep it going. Jackson shows how custom can make violence seem normal.

questions.stem: What do 'Flower Garden' and 'The Renegade' both suggest about communities?
options: They pressure people to conform and punish those who stand apart
They welcome outsiders but turn on members who break the rules
They are kinder than cities, where people ignore one another
They change quickly when one brave person shows them a better way
questions.explanation: Mrs MacLane is frozen out for treating Mr Jones fairly, and Mrs Walpole is surrounded by neighbours eager to punish her dog. In both, the community's approval depends on going along with it.

questions.stem: 'The Tooth', 'The Villager' and 'The Daemon Lover' all explore which idea?
options: How dreams of escape are rewarded with a fresh start
How fragile a person's sense of identity can be
How city life frees women from the expectations of home
How romantic love gives a person a secure sense of self
questions.explanation: Clara cannot recognise herself in a mirror, Hilda slips into another woman's life, and the bride's whole future dissolves when Jamie vanishes. Jackson shows identity as easily lost.

questions.stem: In 'Of Course' and 'After You, My Dear Alphonse', what does Jackson suggest about politeness?
options: It reflects genuine kindness that readers should admire
It is a mask worn mainly by newcomers trying to fit in
It helps characters overcome their prejudices in time
It can hide judgement, prejudice and cruelty
questions.explanation: Mrs Tylor's 'of course' and Mrs Wilson's offers of help are courteous on the surface. Underneath they carry disapproval and racial condescension, which the reader sees and the characters do not admit.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the calm, matter-of-fact tone of 'The Lottery'?
options: It warns the reader from the first line that someone will be killed
It distances the reader so that the stoning feels unimportant
It makes the violent ending more shocking because it seems so ordinary
It shows that the narrator disapproves strongly of the villagers' ritual
questions.explanation: Jackson describes the lottery in the same plain voice as the weather and the gossip. Because nothing seems wrong, the reader is unprepared for the stoning.

questions.stem: Early in 'The Lottery', boys fill their pockets with stones and build a pile in the square. What technique is this?
options: Flashback
Hyperbole
Allusion
Foreshadowing
questions.explanation: The stones look like part of a children's game, but they prepare for the ending. On rereading, the detail becomes chilling.

questions.stem: Many of Jackson's endings stop suddenly, without explaining what happens next. What is the main effect?
options: The reader is left certain about what the characters will do
The unease stays with the reader, who must fill the gap
The reader is given a moral that explains the story's meaning
The characters are shown to have learned their lessons
questions.explanation: 'Charles', 'The Daemon Lover' and 'The Lottery' all end on a final shock or an open question. The lack of explanation makes the disturbing ideas linger.

questions.stem: Why is the reader likely to guess the truth in 'Charles' before Laurie's mother does?
options: Laurie's own rude behaviour at home matches what 'Charles' does
The teacher writes a letter saying Charles is really Laurie
Laurie admits halfway through that he made Charles up
Laurie's father tells the reader the truth in the opening
questions.explanation: Laurie talks back and is rude at home while describing Charles's misbehaviour at school. The mother misses the link, which creates dramatic irony and much of the story's humour.

questions.stem: Who says, 'Lottery in June, corn be heavy soon'?
options: Tessie Hutchinson, arriving late
Mrs Adams, talking about the north village
Old Man Warner, recalling an old saying
Mr Summers, opening the lottery
questions.explanation: Warner quotes the saying when he hears other villages may give up the lottery. It hints that the ritual began as a superstition about the harvest, a reason the village has mostly forgotten.

questions.stem: What does Old Man Warner's line 'There's always been a lottery' show?
options: He thinks the lottery should be changed to suit modern times
He defends the lottery only because it is a tradition
He has doubts about the lottery but is afraid to say so
He believes the lottery is fair because it is left to chance
questions.explanation: Warner offers no real reason for the lottery beyond the fact that it has always happened. The line sums up the danger of tradition followed for its own sake.

questions.stem: Who cries, 'It isn't fair, it isn't right' at the end of 'The Lottery'?
options: Tessie Hutchinson, as the villagers close in on her
Bill Hutchinson, when his family's name is drawn
Nancy Hutchinson, when she opens her slip of paper
Mrs Dunbar, who cannot run fast enough to join the others
questions.explanation: Tessie's last words protest the injustice, but only now that she is the victim. The story ends: 'and then they were upon her.'

questions.stem: In 'Charles', what does the line 'We don't have any Charles in the kindergarten' reveal?
options: That Charles has left the school and moved to another town
That the teacher has confused Charles with another child in the class
That Laurie's mother has misheard the name of his best friend
That Laurie invented Charles to describe his own bad behaviour
questions.explanation: The teacher's reply is the story's last line. It reveals the truth in one sentence and leaves the mother, and the reader, to put the pieces together.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Jackson shows that ordinary people are capable of great cruelty.' Discuss.
options: This essay will discuss cruelty in The Lottery and Other Stories by Shirley Jackson
In The Lottery, the villagers meet in the square on a sunny June morning
Jackson suggests that cruelty grows out of ordinary routines, not from villains
The Lottery is a famous story by Shirley Jackson that was published in 1948
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and sets up an argument. The others give facts, announce the essay or retell the plot.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'In The Lottery the children collect stones before the lottery starts.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Retell what happens after the children are called back to their families
Explain how the children's game shows violence being passed down as normal
Add the names of every child in the story who collects stones in the square
Describe the size and shape of the stones the children choose for the pile
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what a detail suggests. Linking the children's stones to the way tradition is taught to each generation connects the evidence to Jackson's ideas.
